1142.title: No beings freed (section 25)
1142.hook: the Tathagata doesn't think "I free beings"; there are no beings for him to free

Two neighbors shovel the same snowy sidewalk for an old man down the street. One does it before dawn and never brings it up. The other brings it up at every barbecue for a year. Same snow, same clear path. But the second one carries something extra home: a little ledger. I did that. For him. He owes me. Section twenty-five of the Diamond Sutra goes after that ledger at the very top, with the Tathagata, the awakened one himself.

segments.voice: The Buddha asks Subhuti, in paraphrase: does the Tathagata think, I have set beings free? Don't think so, Subhuti. That's a strange thing to deny, since the sutra opened with a vow to free all beings. The reason: there is no being whom the Tathagata has set free. If he thought that way, he'd be holding on to an idea of a self, a being, a living soul, a person, the same four ideas the sutra has been cutting since section three. Notice what goes and what stays. The help doesn't vanish. The helper's tally does. Then a turn the sutra loves. What is called a self is taught by the Tathagata as no self, and yet ordinary, unlearned people hold on to it. And those ordinary people are not ordinary people either; they're only called that. Nobody is written off as hopeless, not even the person still clinging. The label gets cut along with the self. In section three, the bodhisattva vowed to lead all beings to nirvana while knowing that no being is led. Section twenty-five points that same vow at the Tathagata. Even at the very top, the rule holds. Way back on day one hundred thirty-seven, you met giving without a receipt; here it is, all the way up. Some Mahayana teachers describe a gift as clean when the giver, the gift and the one who receives are all held lightly. A help that keeps no ledger has nothing to collect, and nobody is left owing.

1143.title: Form and sound (section 26)
1143.hook: those who see me by form or seek me by sound walk the wrong road (as Müller renders the verse)

Outside a bookstore, a line wraps around the block. A famous writer is signing tonight. A young man near the front has waited three hours. He gets his photo, a handshake, the sound of the writer saying his name, and walks away glowing. Then a friend asks what the books are about, and he laughs. He hasn't read them. He saw the face, heard the voice, and missed the writer completely. Section twenty-six of the Diamond Sutra aims this same mistake at the Buddha himself.
screen: `A LINE AROUND THE BLOCK.` → `A FACE, A VOICE, A PHOTO.` → `HE NEVER READ THE BOOKS.`

segments.voice: The Buddha asks Subhuti whether the Tathagata can be recognized by his bodily marks, the signs tradition says a great being bears. The sutra has asked this before; here it adds a sharp reason for the answer no. If the marks were enough, a wheel-turning king, a world ruler who bears the same marks, would be a Tathagata too. A body can look the part and not be the thing. Then the verse. In paraphrase: those who see me by my form, and those who follow me by my voice, have set out on a wrong road. They will not see me. Form is what the eye catches, sound what the ear catches. Both are real, and both are the outside. The second half of the verse is easy to skip. The Buddhas are to be seen from the Dharma; their body is the Dharma. And the Dharma's nature isn't something the mind can grab as an object. So the verse closes one road and points down another: you meet the Tathagata where the teaching is lived, not where the outline of a body stands. What the verse doesn't say matters too. A Buddhist temple may hold images and chanting. Read in a room like that, the verse doesn't ask anyone to tear the images down or fall silent. It asks where the looking stops. A statue can be a doorway. The mistake is to stand in the doorway admiring the frame.

1144.title: Not annihilation (section 27)
1144.hook: don't think the bodhisattva destroys things; emptiness is not nothing

Somewhere tonight a college sophomore reads one chapter of Buddhist philosophy, shuts the book, and tells the roommate: nothing is real. So the dishes don't matter. The roommate, who has seen the sink, has thoughts. It's an old wrong turn, and the Diamond Sutra has been walking right past it for weeks: no self, no marks, no merit held, no teaching owned. Keep cutting like that and someone will call the whole thing a wrecking ball. In section twenty-seven, the Buddha blocks that road by name.
screen: `NOTHING IS REAL, SO NO DISHES.` → `ALL THAT CUTTING.` → `A ROAD BLOCKED BY NAME.`

segments.voice: The sutra has cut almost everything a person could hold: a self, the bodily marks, merit, the teaching itself, even the raft. A listener could decide the bodhisattva's job is to tear things down. So, in paraphrase, the Buddha tells Subhuti: don't think the highest awakening was reached through the marks. And let no one tell you that those on the bodhisattva path teach the destruction or annihilation of anything. Not of a single thing. The cutting was never demolition. This isn't a new idea dropped in at the end. In an early discourse, the Buddha tells a monk named Kaccana that everything exists is one extreme, and nothing exists is the other. The Tathagata teaches by the middle, without going to either. It's the middle way you've met many times on this path, and section twenty-seven stands on the same ground. When the sutra says a thing has no fixed self, it hasn't said the thing is gone. Empty, in this teaching, means empty of a fixed, separate core, not empty of being here. A cup that is only so called still holds the tea. The bodhisattva who frees no beings is still at work helping them. So the roommate is right, and so, in a way, is the sutra. Nothing is fixed. The dishes are still real. And somebody still has to wash them.

Where does a good deed go once it's done? Some of us file it. A volunteer shift in one drawer, a favor for a friend in another, and on a bad night we open the cabinet and count. Proof that we're decent. Buddhists have a word for the good that flows from good actions; in English it's usually called merit. Section twenty-eight of the Diamond Sutra doesn't say merit is fake. It says something stranger about what a bodhisattva does with it.

segments.voice: It starts with a comparison the sutra has used before, with a new winner. One bodhisattva fills worlds as many as the sands of the Ganges with jewels and gives them all away. Another comes to a patient acceptance that all things are without a self and unborn. The second, the Buddha says, makes the greater merit. A heap of jewels loses to a quiet change of mind. And yet a bodhisattva does not take hold of merit. The good is made. It isn't grabbed. Subhuti asks a fair question, in paraphrase: shouldn't a bodhisattva gain merit? The answer threads a needle. Gain it, yes. Take hold of it, no. It is gained, and that's exactly why it isn't to be held, and why it's only called merit gained. Merit is real enough to make, and too alive to keep in a drawer. Back on day one hundred forty-three you met the dedication of merit, and in some Buddhist communities a sitting or a chant still ends that way: whatever good came from this, may it go out to others. The merit is made, then handed on before anyone can count it. It's like a river running through a farm. The water is real, the crops drink it, and nobody owns the river. A filing cabinet fills up and waits to be opened. A river fills the field and keeps moving.

A map app runs on two questions. Where are you? Where are you going? A blue dot, a line, a time to arrival, and at the end a cheerful voice: you have arrived. A few minutes later, a new destination. Whole days can be lived inside that blue dot, always on the way, rarely there. The Diamond Sutra opened with the Buddha on the move, walking into town for alms and back again. Now, near the end, section twenty-nine seems to erase the whole walk.

segments.voice: The Buddha tells Subhuti, in paraphrase: if anyone says the Tathagata comes or goes, or stands, or sits, or lies down, that person hasn't understood what I teach. Those are the ordinary shapes of a body's day, and the Tathagata isn't to be pinned to any of them. But we watched him do every one. Back in section one he walked to town with his bowl, ate, came back, washed his feet and sat down. The sutra isn't taking that back. The body walked. The question is whether the one called Tathagata is that walking. The sutra's reason: the Tathagata doesn't go anywhere and doesn't come from anywhere, and that is exactly why he is called the Tathagata. The sutra hands the title its own meaning. Not a traveler who arrived somewhere special, not a visitor who will one day leave. What the name points to was never on the road. It's the cut from the verse about form and sound, one step deeper: not the body's shape, and not its movements either. So much of a life is spent in transit, in the head if not on the road. Almost there. Not yet. Next. Section twenty-nine doesn't tell anyone to stop walking. The dishes still need doing and the bus still leaves at eight. It points at something in the middle of all the walking that isn't going anywhere.

Late afternoon, and the light comes sideways through a kitchen window. Suddenly the air, which looked empty, is full. Specks drift, turn, flare and vanish. They were there the whole time; the light just caught them. A child on a beach makes the same discovery in reverse. She builds a castle, proud of every tower, and an hour later the tide makes it sand again. Which one was it really? Section thirty of the Diamond Sutra blows that question up to the size of a world.
screen: `SIDEWAYS LIGHT, FULL AIR.` → `A CASTLE BECOMES SAND.` → `WHICH ONE WAS IT?`

segments.voice: The Buddha asks Subhuti, in paraphrase: suppose someone ground a whole vast world system down to dust, finer and finer. Would that heap of specks be many? Many indeed, Subhuti says. Then his reason, and it's a strange one. If the heap were a real thing in itself, the Buddha would not have called it a heap. What's taught as a heap of specks is taught as no heap, and that's why it's called a heap of specks. He turns the same blade on the world. The world system the Tathagata speaks of is not a world system; that's why it's called a world. Why say this? Because if a world really existed as one solid thing, Subhuti says, that would be a grasping at a lump: taking a heap of parts as one fixed whole. The Buddha answers that this grasping at a lump can't truly be put into words. It isn't a thing. Yet ordinary people get hold of it anyway. The mind is a lump-maker. My whole life. This entire mess. Everything is falling apart. Each feels like one solid block. Section thirty grinds the block gently into specks, and then won't let you make the specks into solid little blocks either. Neither the world nor the dust is the final, fixed thing. What's left is closer to that kitchen air: full, moving, and lit.

segments.voice: If there's a window with sun nearby, find the angle where the air shows its specks and watch them drift; if not, close your eyes and let the mind's own pictures drift the same way. 1148.title: Views of self (section 31)
1148.hook: views of self and being are not views; so they are called views
1148.howItsDone: Mahayana teachers read section 31 of the Diamond Sutra as a warning not to turn the teaching of no self into one more view to defend; students meet it in chanting, study and meditation on how views are held.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dust and worlds: a world ground to specks, and neither world nor dust a fixed thing. Your line: a world of dust.

Two friends walk out of a movie. One says, that was brilliant. The other says, that was a mess. By the parking lot, it's no longer about the movie. Each is defending something closer to home: my taste, my judgment, me. A view started as a way of seeing a film and became a wall to stand behind. Section thirty-one of the Diamond Sutra goes after the view under all the others, the view of a self. And it doesn't swap it for a better view. It does something quieter.
screen: `BRILLIANT. A MESS.` → `NOT ABOUT THE MOVIE NOW.` → `THE VIEW UNDER THE VIEWS.`

segments.voice: The Buddha asks Subhuti, in paraphrase: if someone said the Tathagata taught a view of a self, a being, a living soul, a person, would they be speaking rightly? No, says Subhuti. What the Tathagata taught as a view of self is taught as no view, and that is why it's called a view of self. The same four ideas the sutra has cut since its opening sections come back one last time, and this time it isn't the self being cut. It's the view of it. Then the Buddha says that one who sets out on this path should know all things, see all things, and trust all things in such a way that they don't hold on to even an idea of a thing. And of course: an idea of a thing is no idea; that's why it's called an idea. Even the sutra's own teaching about no self is not a new belief to clutch. Look back at the week. No beings freed: help without the ledger. Form and sound: not the face or the voice. Not annihilation, and still not nothing. Merit not held. Neither coming nor going. Dust and worlds. Now views of self. Every day the blade had the same edge. It doesn't throw away beings, bodies, merit or worlds. It takes away the grip. Today it reaches a deeper one: the grip on being right about who we are.
screen: `DID HE TEACH A VIEW OF SELF?` · `NO VIEW, SO CALLED A VIEW.` · `NOT EVEN AN IDEA OF A THING.` · `THE WEEK: THE GRIP, NOT THE THING.` · then, large: `SO-CALLED VIEWS.`

segments.voice: Pick up one opinion you hold firmly, about a person, a habit, a team, or yourself, and let it sit in your mind like a stone in an open palm. Notice where it presses: the jaw, the chest, the hands. Don't drop it and don't argue with it; just loosen the fingers, and let the breath move around it.

Your line: so-called views. A view held in an open palm, not a fist. That's day one thousand one hundred forty-eight, and that's the week.
